365.title: Esau runs to meet him (Genesis 33:1–11)
365.hook: Jacob fears revenge, but his brother runs, embraces him, and weeps
365.carry: to see your face is like seeing god
365.howItsDone: Christians often read Jacob and Esau's meeting alongside the parable of the prodigal son, and churches use both when teaching about reconciliation between estranged family members.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a night at the river Jabbok, a new name, Israel, and a limp. Your line was wrestle till the blessing. What question did you hold onto? Day three hundred sixty-five.

Morning. Jacob is limping. He looks up, and there it is, the thing he has dreaded for twenty years: Esau, coming across the land with four hundred men. Jacob lines up his family, the servants and their children in front, Leah and her children next, Rachel and little Joseph at the very back, where they'll be safest. Then he walks out ahead of all of them, alone, and bows to the ground. Seven times. Each bow a little closer. Everyone has a version of this walk: the call you've avoided for years, the door you have to knock on, the person you wronged, coming toward you, and you can't read their face.
screen: `FOUR HUNDRED MEN.` → `THE FAMILY IN RANKS.` → `SEVEN BOWS.`

segments.voice: And then Esau runs. In the King James Bible: "And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept." No speech. No list of grievances. The brother who once said he would kill Jacob runs to him. Genesis doesn't explain what changed in Esau. It doesn't tell us whether he forgave slowly over twenty years or all at once on the road. The sources are silent, and the silence is part of the gift. Jacob keeps pressing his presents on him, the herds he sent ahead. Esau says, "I have enough, my brother; keep that thou hast unto thyself." Jacob insists. And then he says the line that gives us today's carry: "I have seen thy face, as though I had seen the face of God, and thou wast pleased with me." Remember yesterday: Jacob named the river Peniel, face of God, because he wrestled there and lived. Now he sees God's face again, this time in a brother's face that he expected to be furious and found full of welcome. Christian readers often hear another story inside this one. When Jesus tells of the prodigal son, the father sees his son far off, and runs, and falls on his neck, and kisses him: almost the same words. Many hear the father in Esau. And the story stays honest about the next part. The brothers don't move in together. They part kindly and live in different places. Reconciliation here is a real embrace, not a perfect ending.
screen: `ESAU RUNS, AND THEY WEEP.` · `I HAVE ENOUGH, MY BROTHER.` · `GOD'S FACE IN A BROTHER'S FACE.` · `THE PRODIGAL'S FATHER RUNS TOO.` · then, large: `AS THOUGH I HAD SEEN THE FACE OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make the first move toward a rift. Settle, and breathe. Picture someone you've drifted from, or wronged, or been wronged by. See their face as clearly as you can. Notice what you expect to find in it: anger, coldness, nothing. Then picture it softening, even a little. You don't have to fix anything in two minutes. Just choose one small first step you could take, a text, a wave, a kind word. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Peniel. The place Jacob named face of God after wrestling there, the same word he uses when he sees that face again in Esau's welcome.
Your line: to see your face is like seeing god. Today, look properly at one face you usually rush past, and let it be a gift. Day three hundred sixty-five.

trapdoor: what you thought: a happy reunion between two brothers.
what it means: the man Jacob wronged runs to him first, and Jacob says seeing his face is like seeing God's.

what a scholar hears: the word face runs through chapters 32 and 33: Jacob's gifts go before his face, he sees God face to face at Peniel, then sees Esau's face as God's. Genesis ties the river and the reunion together.

366.title: The coat (Genesis 37:1–11)
366.hook: a favored son, a many-colored coat, and dreams that anger his brothers
366.howItsDone: The Joseph story is often taught to children through the coat, and preachers use Genesis 37 to talk about favoritism and envy in families.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Esau ran to meet his brother at Peniel, and Jacob said, to see your face is like seeing God. Did you make a first move toward anyone? Day three hundred sixty-six.
screen: `TO SEE YOUR FACE IS LIKE SEEING GOD.`

segments.voice: In some family group chats, everyone knows who the favorite is. The one whose birthday gets the bigger post. The one whose news gets three heart emojis from Dad. Nobody says it. Everybody sees it. Jacob's family has a favorite too, and his name is Joseph. He's seventeen. He's Rachel's first son, born when Jacob was old, and Rachel, the wife Jacob loved most, has died. The brothers are out with the flocks every day. Joseph is with them, and he brings back a bad report about them to their father. Today Joseph's story begins. It starts with a piece of clothing.
screen: `EVERYONE KNOWS THE FAVORITE.` → `JOSEPH, SEVENTEEN.` → `A BAD REPORT.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age: and he made him a coat of many colours." Many colors is the famous version, but translators aren't sure what the Hebrew phrase means. Some modern translations say a long robe with sleeves, the kind of thing you wear when you don't do field work. The same Hebrew words turn up again in Second Samuel, for a robe worn by a king's daughter. Either way, everyone could see it. The coat said, out loud and every day, this one is different. And the brothers respond exactly the way you'd expect: "they hated him, and could not speak peaceably unto him." Then Joseph has dreams. In the first, the brothers' sheaves of grain bow down to his sheaf. In the second, the sun, the moon and eleven stars bow down to him. And he tells them. Both times. Even Jacob rebukes him for the second one. But the text adds a quiet line: the brothers envied him, but his father kept the saying in mind. Notice that nobody in this scene is innocent. A father playing favorites. A teenager who can't keep his dreams to himself. Brothers whose resentment is hardening into something worse. Genesis doesn't make anyone a villain yet. It just shows the cost of favor, paid by everyone in the house. Remember Isaac loved Esau, and Rebekah loved Jacob. Jacob grew up in a house of favorites, and now he builds another one.
screen: `LOVED MORE THAN ALL HIS CHILDREN.` · `MANY COLORS, OR LONG SLEEVES?` · `THEY COULD NOT SPEAK PEACEABLY.` · `SHEAVES AND STARS BOW DOWN.` · then, large: `THE SON OF HIS OLD AGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice favoritism around you. Settle, and breathe. Think of a family, an office, a team or a classroom you're part of. Who is the favorite? Who is the one who never quite gets the coat? Now the harder part: is there anywhere you are the one handing out coats? Don't judge yourself harshly. Just see it. Then think of one small way to even things out tomorrow. If you pray, you can ask for a fair heart. The bell holds the time.
The coat. The special robe Jacob gave Joseph, his favorite son: a sign of love, and a daily reminder to his brothers that they were loved less.
Your line: favor has a cost. Today, give a little extra attention to the person in the room who usually gets the least of it. Day three hundred sixty-six.

what it means: a visible sign that one son was loved more, worn every day in front of the brothers who weren't.
what a scholar hears: ketonet passim turns up again for Tamar, King David's daughter, in 2 Samuel 13. translators differ: a long-sleeved or full-length robe, or the many colors of the King James.

367.title: Into the pit (Genesis 37:12–36)
367.hook: his brothers throw him in a pit and sell him for twenty pieces of silver
367.carry: the pit is not the end
367.howItsDone: Christian tradition has often read Joseph's betrayal as a foreshadowing of Jesus, betrayed for silver, and the story is used in teaching about families torn apart by envy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the coat: a favored son, a father who couldn't hide it, and brothers who couldn't speak kindly to him. Your line was favor has a cost. Who did you notice getting overlooked? Day three hundred sixty-seven.

Jacob sends Joseph on an errand: go and see if your brothers are all right, and bring me word. The brothers are far from home with the flocks, a long walk north. Joseph goes, and gets lost, and a stranger has to point him the right way. Picture the brothers on a hillside, squinting at a figure in the distance. They can tell it's him from a long way off. Maybe it's the coat. One of them says, here comes the dreamer. And before he even reaches them, they've decided what to do.
screen: `AN ERRAND FROM HIS FATHER.` → `SEEN FROM FAR OFF.` → `HERE COMES THE DREAMER.`

segments.voice: Their first plan is murder: kill him, throw him in a pit, say a wild animal ate him, and see what becomes of his dreams. Reuben, the oldest, talks them out of killing him. Throw him in the pit alive, he says, secretly planning to come back and rescue him. So they strip off the coat and throw him in. In the King James Bible: "the pit was empty, there was no water in it." A dry cistern in the ground. Then, the text says, the brothers sit down to eat. Joseph is in the hole, and they have lunch. Years later they'll remember hearing him plead with them. A caravan of traders comes by on its way to Egypt, and Judah has an idea: what profit is there in killing our brother? Let's sell him. So they pull him up and sell him for twenty pieces of silver. Genesis names the buyers as Ishmaelites and also as Midianites, and readers still puzzle over how the two fit together. Reuben comes back, finds the pit empty, and tears his clothes. Then the brothers take the coat, dip it in the blood of a goat, and bring it to Jacob. Remember the goat skins Jacob wore to fool his own blind father? Now a goat fools him. He says an evil beast has devoured Joseph, and refuses to be comforted: I will go down to the grave mourning. And the chapter ends with one more line. Joseph is sold in Egypt, to an officer of Pharaoh named Potiphar. He is alive. The pit was not the end. Some Christian readers hear in this an early echo of Jesus, betrayed by those close to him for pieces of silver.
screen: `KILL HIM, OR THROW HIM IN?` · `AN EMPTY PIT. THEY EAT.` · `SOLD FOR TWENTY PIECES.` · `A COAT DIPPED IN GOAT'S BLOOD.` · then, large: `THE PIT WAS EMPTY, THERE WAS NO WATER IN IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone betrayed by family. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who has been hurt by the people who were supposed to protect them. Maybe someone you know. Maybe it's you. Don't relive the details. Just picture them at the bottom of the pit, and picture a way out, even if you can't see what it is yet. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, hold them in mind with care. The bell holds the time.
Bor. Hebrew for a pit or cistern: where Joseph's brothers threw him before selling him to traders bound for Egypt.
Your line: the pit is not the end. Today, if you know someone in a pit right now, send them one message that says you haven't forgotten them. Day three hundred sixty-seven.

fork.reveal: Judah says: what profit is it if we slay our brother? they sell him for twenty pieces of silver. Judah's story isn't over: he'll stand in this same kind of choice again.

what a scholar hears: the chapter names both Ishmaelites and Midianites as traders, a puzzle readers still discuss; some see two tellings woven together, others read the names as overlapping groups.

368.title: Potiphar's house (Genesis 39)
368.hook: a slave, falsely accused, and yet the Lord was with Joseph
368.howItsDone: Many Christians turn to Genesis 39 in seasons of unfair treatment or unwanted work, and the repeated line "the LORD was with Joseph" is often used in sermons and devotions about God's presence in hard places.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bor: a dry cistern, twenty pieces of silver, and a coat dipped in goat's blood. Your line was the pit is not the end. Who did you hold in mind? Day three hundred sixty-eight.

Some people end up in a job they never chose. A night shift taken because the rent was due. A family business you were drafted into. A first job in a city where you know no one, doing work far below what you hoped for. Now take that and make it far worse. Joseph is barely more than a boy, in a foreign country, and he has been sold. He is a slave in the house of Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard. Nobody from home knows where he is. His father thinks he's dead. And the chapter's first line about him is not what you'd expect.
screen: `A JOB YOU NEVER CHOSE.` → `SOLD, SEVENTEEN, ALONE.` → `POTIPHAR'S HOUSE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "And the LORD was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man; and he was in the house of his master the Egyptian." Notice the order. The Lord was with him, and he was still in his master's house. Being with God did not mean getting out. It meant that, where he was, things went well. Potiphar notices, and puts him in charge of everything he owns. Then Potiphar's wife notices him too. Joseph is handsome, the text says, and day after day she presses him to sleep with her. He refuses, and gives his reason: his master has trusted him with everything, "how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" One day, when the house is empty, she grabs him by his garment. He runs, and leaves it in her hand. Count the garments: his coat was stripped off by his brothers, and now another is left in his master's wife's hand. And again the clothing is used to tell a lie. She tells the household, and then her husband, that Joseph attacked her. Potiphar is furious, and Joseph is thrown into prison. He did the right thing and lost everything again. And then the chapter repeats itself, almost word for word: "But the LORD was with Joseph, and shewed him mercy." The keeper of the prison puts him in charge of the other prisoners. Twice in one chapter, from the top of a house to the bottom of a prison, the same line. Some readers hold onto this chapter for that reason. It doesn't promise Joseph safety. It says, twice, that he wasn't alone where he landed.
screen: `WITH HIM, AND STILL A SLAVE.` · `HOW CAN I SIN AGAINST GOD?` · `ANOTHER GARMENT, ANOTHER LIE.` · `IN PRISON, THE SAME LINE.` · then, large: `THE LORD WAS WITH JOSEPH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do good work where you're stuck. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place in your life you'd leave if you could: a job, a role, a situation that isn't fair. Picture yourself there tomorrow. Now find one small piece of it you could do well anyway, with care, not for anyone's praise. Picture doing it. If you pray, you can ask God to be with you there. If you don't, simply notice that you can bring something good into a place you didn't choose. The bell holds the time.
Potiphar's house. Where Joseph served as a slave, rose to run everything, refused his master's wife, and was falsely accused.
Your line: the lord was with him. Today, in the part of your day you'd most like to skip, do one task as well as you can. Day three hundred sixty-eight.

what it means: God was with him as a slave and as a prisoner. the line doesn't promise escape; it promises company.

369.title: Dreams in prison (Genesis 40)
369.hook: Joseph interprets dreams and asks to be remembered, and is forgotten two years
369.howItsDone: Some Christians read Joseph's long wait in prison as a picture of trusting God through delay, and the words "remember me" are part of Christian prayer through the thief's request in Luke 23:42.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Potiphar's house: a slave who did right, a garment used for a lie, and a prison. Your line was the lord was with him. Which stuck place did you do good work in? Day three hundred sixty-nine.

A covered shift. A reference letter. A friend talked through a terrible night. And the friend says, I won't forget this. Then weeks go by, and nothing. Not a call, not a thank-you. In Pharaoh's prison, two new prisoners arrive: the king's chief butler, the man who served his cup, and the king's chief baker. Both have offended Pharaoh. Joseph, who now looks after the prisoners, is assigned to them. One morning he finds them both looking miserable, and asks the kind of question a jailer doesn't usually ask: why do you look so sad today?
screen: `I WON'T FORGET THIS.` → `THE BUTLER AND THE BAKER.` → `WHY SO SAD TODAY?`

segments.voice: They've each had a dream, and there's no one to explain it. Joseph says, in the King James Bible: "Do not interpretations belong to God? tell me them, I pray you." Notice he doesn't claim the gift as his own. The butler dreams of a vine with three branches, grapes ripening, and himself pressing them into Pharaoh's cup. Joseph says: in three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and give you back your job. Then Joseph asks for one thing. "But think on me when it shall be well with thee." The Hebrew verb is remember: remember me, mention me to Pharaoh, get me out of here. I was stolen from my land, he says, and I've done nothing to deserve this pit. Here, for once, Joseph speaks about what has been done to him. The baker, encouraged, tells his dream: three baskets of bread on his head, and birds eating out of the top one. Joseph doesn't soften it: in three days Pharaoh will lift up your head, from off you. Three days later, on Pharaoh's birthday, it happens exactly so. The butler gets his cup back. The baker is hanged. And then the last line of the chapter, flat as a closed door: "Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him." The next chapter begins two full years later. Some Christian readers hear a far-off echo of this at the cross, where a man dying beside Jesus asks, Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom. That man is answered the same day. Joseph asked, and waited two years with no answer.
screen: `INTERPRETATIONS BELONG TO GOD.` · `THREE BRANCHES: YOUR CUP BACK.` · `THINK ON ME. REMEMBER ME.` · `THE BUTLER FORGOT. TWO YEARS.` · then, large: `YET DID NOT THE CHIEF BUTLER REMEMBER JOSEPH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be patient with being forgotten. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time someone forgot you: a promise not kept, a call not returned, a thank-you that never came. Let it be honest. Joseph was honest; he said, I have done nothing to deserve this. Then breathe out, and set it down for two minutes. And think of one person you may have forgotten, someone who did you a kindness you never followed up. If you pray, you can pray for them both. The bell holds the time.
Joseph. The prisoner who interpreted two dreams, asked to be remembered, and was then forgotten for two years.
Your line: remember me. Today, be the butler who remembers: thank one person you've been meaning to thank. Day three hundred sixty-nine.

what it means: a prisoner who credits God, asks one man to remember him, and waits two years in silence.
what a scholar hears: "lift up your head" is a wordplay. Pharaoh lifts the butler's head to honor him, and the baker's head off him; the same phrase cuts both ways.

370.title: Pharaoh's dreams (Genesis 41:1–40)
370.hook: seven fat cows, seven thin; Joseph plans for famine
370.howItsDone: Christians often point to Joseph's storehouses when teaching about stewardship and wise planning, and many church food banks and savings programs draw on this story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph in prison: a butler, a baker, and Joseph's one request. Your line was remember me. Did you thank someone you'd been meaning to? Day three hundred seventy.

Two full years go by. Then the most powerful man in Egypt has a bad night. Pharaoh dreams he's standing by the Nile, and seven cows come up out of the river, sleek and fat, and graze in the reeds. Then seven more come up after them, thin and ugly, and the thin cows eat the fat ones, and look just as thin as before. He wakes, falls asleep again, and dreams of seven full ears of grain on one stalk, swallowed by seven thin, scorched ones. In the morning he calls every wise man and magician in Egypt. Nobody can tell him what it means. And the butler, standing there holding the cup, suddenly remembers something.
screen: `SEVEN FAT, SEVEN THIN.` → `NOBODY CAN EXPLAIN IT.` → `THE BUTLER REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: The butler confesses: I remember my faults this day. There was a young Hebrew in prison. Pharaoh sends for Joseph at once. And notice the detail: Joseph shaves, and changes his clothes. The young man who keeps losing his garments gets a new one. Pharaoh says, I hear you can interpret dreams. Joseph's answer, in the King James Bible: "It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace." The same move as in prison. Not me. God. Then he explains. The two dreams are one. Seven good years of harvest are coming, and after them seven years of famine so severe that the good years will be forgotten. And the dream came twice, he says, because God has settled it. But Joseph doesn't stop at explaining. He gives a plan. Find a wise man and set him over the land. During the seven good years, store up a fifth of the harvest, grain in the cities, kept for the famine. Don't spend all of the good years in the good years. Pharaoh looks around his court and says: "Can we find such a one as this is, a man in whom the Spirit of God is?" And he puts Joseph in charge of all Egypt, second only to Pharaoh himself. This morning he was a forgotten prisoner. By the afternoon he runs the country. Christians have read Joseph as a model of faith joined to practical wisdom: he trusts God with the future and still builds the barns. In this chapter, giving God the credit and drawing up a grain plan sit side by side. Joseph does both.
screen: `SHAVED AND NEWLY CLOTHED.` · `IT IS NOT IN ME: GOD WILL ANSWER.` · `SEVEN GOOD YEARS, SEVEN LEAN.` · `STORE A FIFTH FOR THE FAMINE.` · then, large: `A MAN IN WHOM THE SPIRIT OF GOD IS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: save a little for later. Settle, and breathe. Think about what your fat years look like right now: maybe money, maybe energy, maybe time with someone who won't always be around. Then think of a lean year that will likely come: a hard season, a quiet stretch, getting older. What is one small thing you could set aside now? Money, yes, but also patience, friendships, rest. Picture storing it. If you pray, you can ask for wisdom about it. The bell holds the time.
Pharaoh's dreams. Seven fat cows and seven thin, seven full ears and seven scorched: seven years of plenty, then seven of famine.
Your line: plan for the lean years. Today, put a little aside, a few dollars, an hour, a phone call, for a season that will need it. Day three hundred seventy.

what it means: he gives God the credit, then turns a warning into a plan, and a forgotten prisoner runs Egypt by evening.
what a scholar hears: Pharaoh's dreams are set at the Nile, whose yearly flood decided whether Egypt ate. ancient Egyptian texts also remember famines, though none can be tied to Joseph.

371.title: The brothers bow (Genesis 42)
371.hook: his brothers come for grain and don't recognize him; he turns away and weeps
371.howItsDone: Some Christians read Genesis 42 as a story about guilt surfacing years later, and preachers use the brothers' confession to talk about honesty and repentance within families.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pharaoh's dreams: seven fat cows, seven thin, and a prisoner who ended the day running Egypt. Your line was plan for the lean years. What did you set aside? Day three hundred seventy-one.

The good years come, and Joseph fills the storehouses. Then the famine arrives, just as the dreams said, and it reaches far beyond Egypt, all the way to Canaan, where an old man named Jacob is watching his family go hungry. He hears there's grain in Egypt. He tells his sons: why do you just sit there looking at one another? Go down and buy some. Ten brothers go. The youngest, Benjamin, Rachel's other son, stays home. Jacob has already lost one of Rachel's boys. He won't risk the second. So ten men walk into Egypt to stand in line for bread, in front of the governor of the land.
screen: `THE FAMINE REACHES CANAAN.` → `TEN BROTHERS GO DOWN.` → `BENJAMIN STAYS HOME.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Joseph's brethren came, and bowed down themselves before him with their faces to the earth." Years after the dream of the sheaves, here it is. The sheaves are bowing, and Joseph remembered the dreams, the text says. And: "Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew not him." Of course they don't. He was a teenager in a coat. Now he's a grown Egyptian official, shaved, speaking through an interpreter. He speaks roughly to them. He accuses them of being spies. He puts them in custody for three days. Then he lets them go, but keeps one brother, Simeon, bound, until they come back with the youngest. And the brothers, not knowing he understands every word, start talking to each other in their own language. "We are verily guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear." All these years later, the pit is still in the room. Then this: "And he turned himself about from them, and wept." The powerful governor steps away so no one sees his face, cries, and comes back to keep testing them. Why does he test them? Genesis doesn't say. Readers have wondered whether he wants to know if they've changed, or whether he's simply hurt and doesn't know what to do yet. Genesis leaves both open. Look at the week behind us: Esau running to his brother, the coat, the pit, Potiphar's house, the forgotten prisoner, the dreams by the Nile. Under all of it sits a family that broke. And now, in this chapter, the brothers say out loud what they did.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice tears you've hidden. Settle, and breathe. Maybe there was a time you turned away so no one would see you cry: at work, at a funeral, in the car before walking into the house. You don't have to cry now. Just notice what was being carried then, and how long it was carried alone. Then let your shoulders drop. If you pray, you can bring that moment to God. If you don't, simply be gentle with the person you were then. The bell holds the time.
Simeon. The brother Joseph holds back in Egypt, kept bound until the others return with their youngest brother.
Your line: he turned away and wept. Today, if you see someone holding it together in public, give them a little room, and a little kindness. Day three hundred seventy-one.
